How tary Treat A Criminat’s Deap
Bopy In New JerRseY.—While the company as-
sembled at the Sheriff’s dinner at the State Street
House were waiting in the parlor, the subject of
the hanging of Lewis for the murder of Mr. Rowan,
of Princeton, was discussed. It was the opinion
of some that notwithstanding the murderer’s crimes
his body was treated inhumanly after death. It
was taken to Princeton, set up with a club in his
hands and his picture taken, after which it was
brought to this city and the flesh boiled from the
bones by a soap boiler. Dr. Rogers, of this city,
now has the skeleton, and Fowler & Wells, of New
York, the skull. It was hardly an appropriate
subject to discuss before an incoming Sheriff, but
the probabilities are that he will have no such un-
pleasant tasks to perform in superintending the ar-
rangements for legally sending a human being out
of the world.—Zvrenton Emporium.

We have a few thousand skulls; some of pirates,
some of murderers, and some which were of well-
disposed persons, willed to us by their owners.
Weare not aware that the skull of the aforesaid
Lewis is among them. The Hmporiuwm may be in
error on the point. When skulls are sent or
brought to us in a proper condition, we receive
and place them on free exhibition.

Tur Great American Boox.—If we
have not yet produced that great American novel
to astonish the world—which, with Mrs. Stowe in
mind, we do not so soon acknowledge—we have
still enough to be proud of in that wonderful pro-
duct of American scholarship—Webster’s Diction-
ary. There has before been no such dictionary of
any language—not even as the result of those years
of labor which the whole French Academy, a con-
gregation of the best scholarship of France, spent
upon the lexicographical standard of that nation.
It has now stood the test of time, and received in
approval not only that popular verdict which in
the United States has called for over fifty million

copies of the Webster series, but the thorough en-

dorsement of our best scholars, as put forth indi-
vidually and in the pages of the authoritative
periodicals. It is not only, to quote Professor
Stowe, ‘“‘in many respects the greatest literary
work which America has ever produced,”’ but it is
in many respects the greatest literary work pro-
duced in any nation or age.

The great Pictorial, Unabridged, which G. & C.
Merriam (of Springfield) publish, is the prince of
the series. Its 1,840 pages contain 114,000 words
and definitions, and over 3,000 illustrations. When
we consider, in addition, that the valuable prefa-
tory and appended matter comprises the contents
of three or four twelvemo volumes—Prof. Hadley’s
History of the English Language, the Treatise on
Pronunciation, Prof. Wheeler’s Vocabulary of
Fictional Names and Places, the Pronouncing and
Etymological Vocabularies of Greek and Latin,
Scriptural, Geographical and Christian Names, the
Dictionary of Quotations, etc.—the wonder grows
upon us. This is a dictionary worthy to be the
cradle of any literature.—W. Y. Evening Mail.

And this is the magnificent book we give as a
premium for only eight new subscribers to THE
PHRENOLOGICAL JOURNAL; a work which ought
to be found in every family.

Man anp Woman, considered in their
Relations to each other, and to the World. By
Henry C. Pedder. 12mo, pp. 116, tinted paper,
extra Cloth, price $1. Sent free by post. Samuel
R. Wells, publisher, New York.

In this work the author has endeavored to eluci-
date as clearly as possible the fundamental fact,
that there is quite as much evidence of adaptation
and design in the arrangement of sexhood as exist-
ing between man and woman, as there is in any
other aspect under which creative powers manifests
itself to us.

The first three chapters of the work are devoted
to an examination into those phases of reciprocal
sentiment which appeal to us so strongly at every
stage of our experience, and which culminate in
those transcendant joys resulting from a spiritu-
alized affection, and introduce us clearly to an ap-
preciation of marriage, not only as a great moral
necessity, but also as the highest, purest and lofti-
est condition of human life. .

The chapter on the ‘‘ Equality of the Sexes,”’ is
designed mainly to accomplish that which consti-
tutes the most pressing need of modern society,
viz.: a proper appreciation of woman in her true
character as an ennobling influence in our midst;
while the line of argument adopted is intended to
carry the conviction to every honest mind, that, as
her powers and opportunities have hitherto been
smothered by an artificial and imperfect estimate,
the time has now arrived when the sphere of her
uses should be extended, and her whole nature
given an opportunity for its expansion into a true
and noble womanhood instead of remaining the
miserable creature of pads, puffs and ornaments,
which she mainly is.

In the last chapter on the ‘‘ Necessity for a well-
defined Relationship,’’ the aim which the author
has in view is to convey in as concise a manner as
possible, the intimate relationship existing between
the internal man and the external world, and
which renders necessary the utmost watchfulness
on our part with reference to the most trifling in-
fluences which exert themselves on the formation
of character.

Indeed, it may be said, that in a partial sense,
this work embraces some of the most momentous
questions of our sexual relationship, and therefore,
commends itself to all earnest and reflective minds.

Joun Brown, JR.,—son of the martyr—
sends us a crate of delicious grapes, grown on
Kelley’s Island, Lake Erie, at Put-in Bay, near
Sandusky, Ohio. The grapes reached us in good
condition, and were enjoyed by the household.
Mr. Brown has had his share in the struggles and
triumphs of political life, and now enjoys the quiet
of rural pursuits, and these are the fruits of his
patient toil. Thanks thanks, thanks.

counterfeit money. He pretends to have offices in
Nassau and John Sts., N. Y. He uses the name
of Lee, and addresses lithographic letters to ‘‘ Hs-
teemed Friends,’ proposing to sell counterfeit
money. It is anew dodge to catch rogues and to
get money. Those who are caught will be sent to
State’s Prison.

THE ROGUES!
A Woman Arter THE Roaurs.—Having

been requested by several country readers, to call
at sundry advertised places in this wicked city, to
look after swindlers; to ‘‘ collect”? money sent for
$3 watches, $5 sewing machines, cheap jewelry,
etc., and, of late, to have sellers of counterfeit
money arrested, we give the following from the
Tribune, which shows how the matter stands at

present :

A Woman’s Curiosity. The “ Circular’? Swin-
dle Again. Mrs. C., a strong-nerved woman, who
manages a farm 6¢ miles from Corry, Pennsylvania,
stopped in this city yesterday, on her way to St.
Augustine, Florida, and spent several hours in
hunting up the publishers of four or five circulars
which she had received, offering counterfeit money
for sale. She had read in THH TRIBUNE repeated
exposures of the swindlers, and, as she states, hada
strong curiosity to see for herself the men who had
sent the circulars, to ascertain whether they really
had any counterfeit money, and, in fact, to unravel
the whole mystery. Her clear and straightforward
manner of stating her motives and experiences
admitted of no doubt that she had actually made
the singular experiment. She went to a number on
Broadway to which one of the circulars had direct-
ed her, but found at the place an unfinished build-
ing. At No. 58 Liberty St., given in one of the
circulars as the headquarters of ‘‘ Owen Brothers,”
she found a man who claimed to be Mr. Owen. She
applied for the privilege of examining the counter-
feit money which had been offered; but Mr. Owen
very insinuatingly explained the difficulties in the
way of granting such a favor. If she wished to buy,
he would have it sent to her address; he didn’t
keep any in his office; he had another office which
the detectives conldn’t reach; if she would lcave
her money, he would pledge his word of honor
that the ‘‘ queer’? would be sent to her at any place
she might name, But she declined his proposition.

She then visited Room No. 5, No. 52 John 8t.,
whence ‘‘ Wm. J. Ferguson’’ sends out his circu-
lars. Mr. Ferguson was not in, but she found a
very pleasant young man who knew something
about him. She stated her wish to buy counterfeit
money, and the young man thereupon lectured her
earnestly upon the danger and impropricty of any
such venture; Mr. Ferguson might have some of
the ‘‘money ;’’ she oughtn’t to go any further in the
business; but if she would, then he would give her
Mr. Ferguson’s address; or, if she chose, she
might leave the amount of money she wanted to
invest in the counterfeits, and he would see that
they were sent. During 2 lo: ¢ interview she made
no progress beyond that point. Meantime a burly
Southerner came into the room. He was informed
by the young man that he could speak freely, as it
was ‘“‘all right.’? Mrs. C. was prepared to discover
_ in him a confederate of Ferguson ; but finally con-
cluded, from his tone and expressions, that he had
really come, as he said, from a town in Georgia.
He stated frankly that he wanted some of the
“ queer ;”’ that he ‘‘ wore the gray next his heart ;”

that the war had ruined him; that he wanted to
‘¢ shove the stuff among the niggers, and get even
with the Yankees somehow.’’ An arrangement was
made that Ferguson should visit the Southerner at’
his hotel, and conclude arrangements for the trans-
fer of the counterfeits. ‘ But,” the young man took
care to impress upon him, ‘Mr. Ferguson, in order
to protect himself, has always been accustomed to
send the ‘goods’ insuch a way that they can’t be
traced to him, and also to require the money to be
sent to him, in the same'way, beforehand.’ Mrs. C.
then abandoned the investigation, and came to
THE TRIBUNE Office to relate her experience for the
benefit of others.

A subscriber in Steuben Co., N. Y., wishes us to

assist in catehing a swindler. He writes :—

‘“‘T have received from some one in N. Y., who
presumed too much, the enclosed letter, which I
wish to get into the hands of the proper officer»
that the rogue may be properly dealt with. Will you
not please see that the ease is rightly managed? I
will keep the address, and will hold myself in read-
iness to forward a package by express, as directed,
as soon as notified that one is wanted. Or, my
name and address may be nsed by the detective in
eompliance with the instruction, to call at the
rogue’s office. I wish, if it be a fact, that a neigh-
bor of mine is in the business, that he too may be
exposed.”’

' These dealers in counterfeit money are sure to be
caught, sooner or later, and will “fetch up” in
prison, where plain fare and steady employment
will be given them. None but rogues or green-
horns are caught, and such lose their money, and
then are sent to States prison, to meditate, and to
serve the State in useful manual labor.

Purenotoay a Mysrery.—Many per-
sons, when they discover the wonderful accuracy
with which their own character or that of their
friends can be read by a phrenologist, at once con-
clade that the science isa mystery, and that special
gifts are necessary to its successful practice.
Phrenology is a SCIENCE, and good common sense
can learn it as easily as it can master Mathematics,
Geography, Grammar or Music. Those who desire
to study the science with a view'to its practice as a
profession, or to aid them the better to read men
as & means of success in business, or in the various
professions, especially the law and theology, may
be glad to know that we instruct a class every year,
in Theoretical and Practical Phrenology. A circular,
stating topics, time and terms will be sent to appli-
cants, on receiptof stamp. Please address Office of
The Phrenological Journal, New York.

Goop Prns, Goop INK, AND Goop
Paper are necessary to the production of a readable
letter. Those written with a poor pen, with poor
pale ink,—or in pencil,—and on poor paper, are a
sad trial to one’s eyes and good nature. Young
writers for the press are sometimes so inconsider-
ate as to disregard all these things, and to send in
a ‘hasty serall,”’ for the Editor to puzzle his tired
faculties on. O the luxury of receiving plainly
written letters, with name, date, and post-office,
and with something in them! The highest style
in use, for note paper and for envelopes at
present is, those which are perfectly plain. No
embossing, no initial letter, nothing but the plain-
est and finest materials are used by the best class.

Tire at Home; or the Family and its
Members. By William Aikman, D.D. $1.50; gilt
$2.00. 8. R. Wexuzs, Publisher. ;

Harper's Monruty Magazine says:
‘How to break up a family, on how small or great
provocation husband and wife may separate,—this
is the great topic of discussion in American circles.
It is refreshing to turn from these disputes about
divorce to such a book as Life at Home, by Dr.
WiLitaAM AIKMAN (S. R. Wells), the object of
which is to tell how the family may be preserved,
and the husband and wife live happily and cheerily
together. Without any pretence to being a great
book, it is, what is better, a very useful one. Dr.
Aikman, very unministerially, spends no time in
discussing theories of marriage; but, assuming the
fact, drives straight to the practical question, how
it shall be made pure and happy. It is a book of
eminent good sense and still more of eminent good
feeling; and a practical regard to its precepts—
rather a practical acceptance of its kind and loving
spirit—would ,make life at home what it always
should be, an earnest of the home toward which
we all are traveling, and where our eternal life of
love shall be.’’

THE GARDEN.

Who that lives in the country has not a garden ?
Who does not remember the garden of his parental
home? Is there anything which awakens so many
pleasing early recollections as that word GARDEN ?
The word home of course, embraces the kitchen, the
dining-room, the parlor, the dormitory, the play-
ground, the lawn, the orchard and the garden, But
the word garden throws as mellow and rich a light
on the tablet of memory as any other word of the
language, with the exception of the word mother.
Some have a plot of ground with a rough wall to
enclose it, with scraggly bushes, clumps of weeds,
anda few sickly plants, struggling to exist, with
poor culture, and poorer care. It is not of this sort
of garden we would speak, except to work its re-
form. The garden we would have our readers en-
joy is one well-cultured and kept; with its aspar-
agus bed, its strawberry plot, its cherry trees, its
peaches, with tomatoes and all manner of succulent
roots, excellent as food, promotive of health and
happiness. But we must not forget the bed of
pinks and the clump of roses, and the other long
line of things of beauty, which in memory, at least
are a ‘‘joy forever.”

But a garden, with its pleasures and profits, re-
quires care, labor, watching and attention, but does
it not a hundred fold repay the time, trouble, and
expense. He who would enjoy his green peas, and
delicious strawberries smothered in cream, must
begin in season. He can make around his home a
garden, which shall remind him of Paradise.

One of the advantages of a garden is that the | ip
| make a strong appeal to friends and others, by stating

women and children can give it much attention.
It cultivates their taste, brings them into the open
air and sunshine, and what with health and the
domestic feeling which arises from such effort
there are a thousand pleasing associations connect-
with garden-culture.

One great reason why many fail in making a gar-
den pleasant and profitable, is that they fail in prop-
er time to get the requisite seeds, bulbs and roots.
When the days come for making a garden, they put
in 2 little of this and that, such as they may chance
to have, and for want of seeds and roots their gar-
den is a comparative failure. Those who live in the
vicinity of large towns can get a catalogue of vege-
table and flower seeds, and select to their liking,
and be in season with their garden. Those who live
far from opportunities of this kind, can send right
to this city, and by naming what they wish, they
can be purchased and forwarded prepaid by post.
We have received many letters making inquiries for
seeds, and have sometimes announced that we
would send whatever may be required by mail, and
we will do the same the present year. Make out
your list, and inclose the amount you wish to in-
vest, and the return post or express will bring you
just what you wish,—procured at the best seeds-
men’s in New York.

To still encourage gardening, even on a small

scale, we venture the following offer. For three
now subscribers to the PHRENOLOGICAL JOURNAL,
at $3 each, we will send the worth of $2 in garden

| or flower seeds, post-paid to any Post-office in the

Unitcd States. Larger quantities, in same propor-
tion. Address this Office.

A CHANCE To WorK youR PAssaGE.
—Weare often written to by young men who de-
sire to study Phrenology, but are limited in their
pecuniary means. They ask us to furnish them with
something to do in our publishing office, or in the
City of New York, whereby they can earn their
tuition, and money to pay their incidental expenses.
This is seldom convenient, and would not, in one
case in twenty, be either pleasant or profitable to
tbe student or to us. But we now propose a plan
by which any enterprising young man, who may
Wish to acquire a thorough knowledge of Phrenology
by attending our class, can acquire the means for
80 doing, viz., by obtaining subscribers for our
JOURNAL, in his own town, or county. The offer
is this: for Firry NEw SuBSCRIBERS TO THE
PHRENOLOGICAL JOURNAL, at $3 a year, we will
give a Scholarship, entitling its holder to a full
course of instruction in Theoretical and Practical
Phrenology. It does not matter where the sub-
scribers may be located, or who may procure them.
One’s sister might obtain a few, or the whole num-
ber. We will furnish circulars and whatever facil-
ities we can, to aid in obtaining the subscribers.

Those who desire to Study Phrenology, and are dis-
posed to obtain a Scholarship in the way proposed, can

their. object plainly, as follows :

‘“‘T am very anxious to study Phrenology, with a
view to making ita life profession and in order to do
80, I wish to visit New York, and receive a thorough
course of instruction, under competent teachers.
To defray my expenses in this undertaking, I am
trying to obtain a given number of new subscribers
to the American Phrenological Journal, for 1871,
which will entitle me to a Scholarship. Will you
become one of that number, and thus kindly aid
me in this, to me, important matter ?”’

To CorrEesponDENTSs.— We wish to eail
the attention of our correspondents to a few im-
portant points: First, if you desire an answer by
mail, always inelose stampsfor return postage ; and,
if circulars or lists are desired, additional postage
should be enclosed, as in many cases these must be
sent in a separate envelope. Second, be careful and
give full address, name (with title, Mr., Mrs., Miss,
Rey., Dr., etce.), Post-office, County, and State.
“hird, do not write with lead-pencil, or pale ink,
cn little slips of paper; use good, bright ink on
clean, white paper. Fourth, when making remit-
tanees, send post-office order or draft on New
York; when these cannot be obtained, register the
letter, inclosing the amount, in the presence of the
post-master, put on stamps for postage and fifteen
cents worth extra for register fee, and take his re-
ceipt for the letter ; it may then be sent at our risk.
Fifth, when sending post-otfice orders, keep a mem-
orandum of the date, number, and name of the
post-office from which it is issued; this will very
much facilitate the getting of duplicates when nec-
essary. We are constantly in receipt of letters,
imperfect in many of the points alluded to above,
causing delay and disappointment to the sender,
and much trouble and annoyance to the publisher,
If these simple rules are followed, all this will be
avoided.

No Comprtiror. — There are many
Story Papers, many Literary Magazines, many Ag-
ricultural, Mechanical, and Commercial Periodicals,
but there is only one PHRENOLOGICAL JOURNAL.
We have no competitor. There have been several
started in the old world and in the new; but from.
some cause, we are alone in this field. The founders
of this Journal even, are either dead, or have failed, ’
and it is left for their successors, its present sup-
porters, to sustain and carry it on. More money
may be made no doubt, in other directions, but that
is not the chief object of life; we can do this, our
chosen work, and by the co-operation of our num-
erous friends and patrons, sustain ourselves. We
not only exist, thank God, but we actually flourish.

Readers may inundate themselves with all
sorts of printed matter, good, bad, and indifferent,
but their knowledge will not be complete without
the PHRENOLOGICAL JOURNAL. We ask that it be ©
placed in the hands of all who can read.

MEN NoT SATISFIED with their position
in life might secure contentment and success by
studying the science of Phrenology. Many a phy-
sician who has more taste for public speaking and
traveling than for the practice of his profession, and
who would prefer to teach the public ‘‘ how not to
be sick”’ than to spend his life in trying to cure a
few who have become sick, might find phrenology
in connection with physiology pleasant and profit-
able. Many a merchant, teacher, farmer, or me-
chanic, yearns for something that will bring him
pleasantly in contact with mind and serve to give
expansion and liberal culture to his character and
talent. To such, practical Phrenology opens a door
where one can do good and get good. Those de-
siring information on this subject may send for a
circular, entitled, ‘‘ Professional Instruction in
Practical Phremology.’’ Address, with stamp for
return postage, office PHRNOLOGICAL JOURNAL,

A New Lecrurer IN THE FIELD.
Mr. Emmet R. Olcott, just returned from his studies
of the Jaw, in the French and German Schools, has
been induced to describe in popular lectures, what
he saw of life on battle-field and in camp—during
the present war—between the French and the Ger-
mans. Mr. Olcott was bearer of dispatches, under
a ‘‘pass”’ from the Crown Prince of Prussia, and met
with. many narrow escapés, Those who can, should
hear this Young American Orator.

Dress AND CARE OF THE FEET,
showing their natural, perfect shape and construc-
tion; their present deformed condition; and how
flat feet, distorted toes, and other defects are to be
prevented or corrected, with directions for dressing
them elegantly, yet comfortably, and hints upon
various matters relating to the whole subject, with
illustrations. 12mo., pp, 202. Price, $1.25. 8. R.
WELLS, Publisher.

This is a work of over two hundred pages, with
ample illustrations, showing how to dress the feet
to prevent the painful results which come from the
tashionable mode of tightly dressing them, such as
corns, bunions, and the like. Most people who
wish a tidy looking foot, wear shoes that are not
adapted to comfort, and by the time they are
twenty-five years of age, they become crippled from
callosities and deformities, so that all the rest of
their life they must be tortured, or else wear shoes
“that are uncomely.

Several years ago, by reading and observation and

some experience, we learned to have our boots
made to fit the,foot, and have been fortunate enough
to have them so made, that they would fit all
parts of the foot alike, so that we could walk all
day in a pair of new boots, without any part of the
foot being pinched, or made uncomfortable.

Every Shoemaker ought to have this book. Those
who are afflicted with corns and bunions, with dis-
tortions and deformities of the feet, will find hints
and illustrations in this work, which will put them
in the right path for avoiding the purgatory of badly
fitting shoes. Parents should read it, and guard
their children against becoming crippled for life,
by ‘‘ bad feet gear.”

The work is written in a plain, practical manner,
by a man who has had experience in fitting the
feet. He knows what he is writing about, and so
expresses himseli that every person who reads, will
be able to understand, and be instrneted thereby.

NARRATIVE OF MY CAPTIVITY AMONG
THE S1oux INDIANS, with a brief account of Gen-
eral Sully’s Indian expedition in 1864, bearing upon
events vecuring in my captivity. By Fanny Key.
12mo., pp. 285, with portrait of the author. Price,
$2.00. Cincinnati; Wilstach, Baldwin & Company.
Would the reader know something of real life—and
of death--among our N. A. Indians? He may find
it here. A little band of enterprising young mar-
ried people, with their first-born, leave their old
homes and friends in the East, to seek their for-
tunes and a new homein the great West. They
fall into the hands of Indians; several are killed;
husbands, wives, and children are separated and
seattered. The author was captured and kept sey-
eral months by the Sioux, and finally rescued by
soldiers from Fort Sully, and restored to her hus-
band. The narrative is intensely interesting, re-
counting thrilling adventures, and narrow escapes
with life. Also the manners and customs of these
savages — courtship, marriage, avocations, etc., as

. observed from the stand point of a civilized and

educated white woman.

SHORT-HAND WRITING, OR PHONOGRAEHY? Ans.
In reply to this, we may simply state, that those
who wish to learn from Pitman, will need the
Reporter’s Companion. If from Graham, he should
obtain Grabam’s Hand-book of Phonography. If
from Munson, the Complete Phonographer will
furnish everything necessary for a course of study.

These are the principal instruction books before
the public. They claim to be of equal merit, and
there are good reporters using each system. Each
reporter generally likes best the system he has
learned, though persons have occasionally changed

from one to another,
Constant practice for two hours daily, will en-

able a persevering student to obtain a good prac-
tical knowledge of short-hand, and attain to a speed
of perhaps seventy-five words per minute, in the
course of a few months; after which = diligent
daily practice only, is necessary, to enable him to
report verbatim, an ordinary sermon or speech.

PHONOGRAPHY, or SHORT-HAND WRI-
TING.—Whose system — Pitman’s, Graham’s or
Munson’s—is Best? In answering, we may state,
that some of our best reporters write after either,
or all three. Mr. Pitman, ofEngland, is the origin-
ator, or, we may say, the inventor of Phonography,
or Phono-Stenography, and all the different phases
of Phonography are based on it. His brother in
America does not follow all the changes which the
inventor has from time to time introduced. Hun-
dreds have learned and practiced Pitman’s system.
Mr. Graham introduced certain improvements, by
which it is claimed greater rapidity in reporting is
possible, and many prefer Graham. Still later, Mr.
Munson conceived that he could simplify and im-
prove on both Pitman and Graham. He worked
out his ideas; put them into book form; and now
we have also his instruction book. It is our opin-
ion, that a student may become a thoroughly com-
petent reporter, by following either. We cannot
give special preference to one, to the exclusion of
the others. We repeat, among the fifty or more
reporters whom we have taught, and employed
during the last twenty years, the best, read and
writes each other’s notes with almost equal facility.
It is perfectly safe therefore, for a student to take
up either Pitman, Graham, or Munson, and follow
him. We give titles and prices of instruction books
as follows:

Munson’s Complete Phonographer, $2.25; Gra-
ham’s Hand-Book of Phonography, $2.25; Graham’s
First Phonographic Reader, $1.75; Graham’s Sec-
ond Phonographic Reader, $2.00; Graham’s Phon-
ographic Dictionary, $5.00; Pitman’s Manual of
Phonography, $1.25; Pitman’s Reporter’s Com-

panion, $1.50; Pitman’s Phrase Book, $1.25; Pit-—

man’s Phonographic Reader, 40 cts.; Handsome
Reporting Case for Phonographic Copy-Books, $1;
Phonographic Copy-Book, 15 cents.

Any of which will be sent post-paid by return
mail, on receipt of price. Address this office.
Should written instructions be desired by learners
the same may be promptly obtained by addressing
the publisher of this Journal.

Toe RuraL CLtus oF New Yorn.—
At the Metropolitan Hotel, on Tuesday evening,
there was a company of gentlemen gathered
for the purpose of uniting in one social body 4
majority of the intelligent men in and around New
York who feel specially interested in rural affairs.
There has not been for many years, if ever, in the
metropolis of this great producing continent, any
society distinctly horticultural. The Farmers’ Club
of the American Institute, popular as it is, and
yalued as its proceedings are by a very large class,
does not claim to answer this requirement. But
the deficiency so long felt is at last supplied. At
the meeting referred to, which was a sequel to sev-
eral informal ones, a complete organization of
‘“‘The Rural Club of New York” was effected by
the adoption of a constitution and the choice of
the following officers: President—Horace Greeley ;
Vice-Presidenits—N. C. Ely, D. D. T. Moore, J. V.
C. Smith; Recording Secretary—J. B. Lyman;
Corresponding Secretary—A. B. Crandell; Hxecutive
Commitiee—F. M. Hexamer, P. T. Quinn, F. D.
Curtis, C. D. Bragdon; Treaswrer—H. T. Williams.

The leading features of the Club are :—1. Special
taste for rural affairs on the part of its members.
2. Each member may invite two friends, and these
may be ladies. 3. The sessions are to be timely in
the character of the subjects diseussed. Thus: In
April, flowers will be the topic, and strawberries in
June; the August session will be a peach discus-
sion, and a month later the talk will be of pears.
4, Strangers of distinction, and farmers from dis-
tant States will be the guests of this Club. 5. Only
one topic will be taken up at a session, and the in-
tention is to make that discussion full and exhaust-
ive, anda report of it may be expected to give a
complete summary of the best that is now known
on that subject. 6. There are to be but four regu-
lar sessions in a year, and these will be made of tho
greatest value to those who are seeking for exact
and practical knowledge in farming and horticul- .
ture. Similar associations ought to be formed in
every city and in every village. Let this ball be
kept in motion.

Woman in France, Germany and in |

America.—Iq noticing our New Book on MAN AND
Woman, Th»? American Christian Review says :—
“We are pleased with the spirit of this little book.
The chapters on ‘ Marriage the True Order of Life,’
and the ‘Necessity for a Well-Defined Relation-
ship,’ we heartily indorse. In discussing the ideal
relation of the sexes, the author says:
itis a beautiful, impassionate woman ministering
to a life of ease and indulgence. In France, if we
are to credit French novels, a feverish, excitable
creature carrying the finest metaphysics into her
Jove, and yet wholly incapable of self-control and
common sense. In Germany the principle idealizes
itself in the two remarkable contrasts of a broad-
faced Hausmutter devoting herself to cooking good
dinners and getting up the family linen, and the
esthetic soul breathing the deepest longing and the
highest aspirations with holes in her stockings.’
(We had almost written ‘hrough holes in her hose.)
The American ideal, however, is higher than buck-
wheat cakes or universal suftrage, and invests the
relation with a sanctity hallowed by Christ’s first
miracle,”’

Oxssects or Lirz.—‘‘ As immortal be-
ings, it is disgraceful for us to suppose, as many
apparently do, that we are placed in this world
merely for the gratification of our appetites and

the propagation of the human race. True, there
are certain conditions with which this view of the
matter may be surrounded, which are caleulated to
suggest to us much that is beautiful and true con-
cerning the ends for which we were created; but
to confine our ideas to this purely carnal view is
low und groveling in the extreme. The more com-
prehensive the mind of the student, and the more
perfect his knowledge both of nature and revela-
tion, the more evident it must be to him that the
main purpose of the Almighty in the creation of
the universe was and is the formation of a heaven
out of the human race.’’—H. C. Pedder, in Manand
Woman.

GAMBLERS, IMPOSTORS, QUACKS, SWINDLERS. |
We receive many letters from all parts of the
country, enquiring as to this or that lottery, scheme,
project, or ‘‘ benevolent enterprise,’’ in which
money, jewelry, remedies, etc., are offered for the
consideration of money. It is scarcely worth while
to mention the real or assumed names of the num-
erous pests, parasites, and vampires, who cheat,
swindle, or rob all who come within their reach.
Among the most wicked, we may name “ THE
Union Hospitat oF N. Y. City, under the con-
trol of an European Faculty.”” Dr. 8. Holman,
examining and contracting Agent; Prof. J. R.
Randolph, President; W. B. Taylor, Sec. These
are the rogues who operated not long ago, under
the names of Harper, Wilson & Co., Isaac Robin-

One Ellis, a cunning rascal, has started a cheap
jewelry concern, in which he sells what he calls
‘“Mitton Goup.’’ The stuff is made of Brass,
washed with a very thin coating of Gold. It is
manufactured on a large scale, and is bought by
negroes, servant girls, and others of this class. The
fraud consists in his giving it a name, intending
to deceive the purchaser. Hair dyes, whisker
growing grease, all-healing ointments, and the var-
ious sorts of medicated bitters, cod liver oils, with
all the so called remedies, for ‘‘indiscreet young
men,’’ may be classed among the quack swindles.
O. Phelps Brown, Howard Association, Dr. Kline,
Dr. Earl, the Anatomical Museum, and numerous
“no cure no pay’’ doctors are in the same boat.
Isis the duty of every good citizen to catch and
punish every villain, found preying on the innocent.
Shut them up, put them at hard work till they re-
form. An extensive business has been done of late
in bogus money, or sawdust. A few arrests, con-
victions, and sentences to prison have been made,

Panel thieves have been scattered, and will no
doubt, soon be found plying their vocation in some
other way. Ifmore stringent measures are not adopt-
ed for ridding the country of criminals, they will
soon have matters their own way. Let us shut up
the grog shops, open day and evening schools, give
employment to all we can, teach, preach and prac-
tice real Philanthropy, enforce the laws on the
lawless, and then crime will diminish, circumstan-
ces will improve.

Buitp1nge Hovsres.—When about it,
build a good house,
selected. Do not build in a swamp, or a quag-

Let the location be properly

mire, which cannot be thoroughly drained, and
where you will be shaken to death with ague and
burned by fever, nor on the top of Whirlwind
Hill, where clapboards, shingles and fences may be

blown away. But place your house with reference
to health, to scenery—a fine landscape is always
charming, and exalts the senses and the sentiments.
Have a sea, lake, river or mountain view when you
can, with a ‘‘ look-out’’ on the sunny side. Have
shrubs and vines near, but not too near, the house;
with larger trees in the distance. Be sure of pure
air and plenty of good water, within easy reach.
Having secured the best possible location, the next
thing is to procure the best plan, or design for just
such a house as you need. If only a log house or
a shanty be desired, reference should be had to
health, cost, convenience, ete. And if a permanent
dwelling be sought, no pains should be spared to
secure all desirable advantages; books should be
studied; plans examined; an architect consulted;
materials and cost ascertained, and decided on, be-
Jore laying the foundation. Will you build of
wood, brick, stone, or concrete? Having settled
which of these, plans may be easily settled. If
concrete is to be the building material, you must
be sure to have plenty of field or other stone, for a
foundation—perfectly under-drained--with plenty
of gravel, sand and lime. If materials be of the
right sort, properly mixed and put up, a cheap,
durable and healthful house of any shape or size
may be built. But, it is better for those inexperi-
enced in this thing, to try an experiment on a small
scale before venturing on a large one. Build a
poultry-house, an ice-house, smoke-house, etc., of
concrete, and learn how it works. If these prove
satisfactory, and the materials be cheap and at
hand, a first-class dwelling may be ventured on.
In any event, one should inform himself thorough-
ly as to all the questions involved. by ‘reading
up’’ the whole subject, that he may have the best
experience of all who have published their views
on building and architecture. Of late years many
of our best horticultural and agricultural journals
have published many excellent designs for dwel-
lings, churches, school-houses, ete., by which the
public taste has been much improved. In anew
country like ours, thousands of buildings will be
erected every year, and it is important that all the
conditions necessary to make a house and home
just what it ought to be, should be carefully con-
sidered. Itis estimated that a considerable num-
ber of our most fashionable and expensive houses
in cities are built over old swales and sink holes,
which have been filled up, rather than properly
drained; and that in these localities the health of
residents is the exception, rather than therule’ It
would be well for those who would live healthfully

and long, to look carefully at both location and
foundation, before investing, even in a city lot.

On another page we give a condensed list of the
best: works on architecture, with prices. We com-
mend the expenditure of a few dollars for such
valuable information as may be thereby obtained,
before launching out in any kind of house build-
ing.

A friend of ours recently paid over $250 for works
containing plans, etc., and has never regretted the
outlay.

THe Wesr Wisconsin Ramway.—Our
readers will find on our outside cover an advertise-
ment of the West Wisconsin Railway, and the
advantages presented by its bonds as a means of
investment. The general features of the Road are
there pretty well outlined. It is only 154 miles in
length, extending across Wisconsin from Tomada,
in the centre of the State, to the flourishing city of
St. Paul; and yet, it is fully 100 miles shorter than
the present route by way of Prairie du Chien. It
is, in fact, the air-line route between St. Paul and
Milwaukee and Chicago, and will be the favorite
channel for that vast trade which ebbs and flows
between the Lake ports and that vast region of our
new Northwest that finds its market in St. Paul.
The local traffic, too, will be no less sure and prof-
itable. One hundred and twenty miles of the road
are completed and in operation, and the amount of
business done on them during the past few months
has proved that local traffic alone will be sufficient
to pay all expenses, and the interest on the con-
struction debt.

The Bonds are as secure, probably, as a railroad
bond can be made. They are a first mortgage, not
only upon the road itself, but upon a land grant of
6,400 acres per mile, or over 1,000,000 in the aggre-
gate. These lands are very choice, and have been
estimated by competent surveyors to be worth
from five to seven million dollars. There is no
doubt that with judicious management they will
be more than sufficient to redeem the bonds; so,
the purchasers of the Bonds, at least, are. safe,
while they make a profit of about 9 per cent. per
anpnnm. The bonds are payable in gold in 1885,
and bear interest in gold at seven per cent.

CounrEerrerr Monsey DxraLers.—A
large number of wicked swindlers are engaged in
sending out circulars, offering to supply any
quantity of the ‘Stuff,’ at a low price. Here is
the report of a case of arrest and conviction, which
will please all honest men:

The Sawdust Counterfeiters.—A little term in the
Penitentiary—The Hon. Abe H. Hummel’s opinion
of a New Hampshire man—Justice Dowling’s Hint
to the Nassau Street Gang.—Melvin L. Gove, a

Inerchant of Seabrook, N. H., received a printed
circular from Owens & Co., of 58 Liberty street
and 78 Nassau street, informing him that they
manufactured counterfeit money. Mr. Gove,
though a churchman, hastening to this city, sought
Owens & Co., and invested $15. The firm prom-
ised to send the counterfeit stuff by express. He
went, and the next express took aC. O. D. pack-
age for ‘*‘ Melvin L. Gove, Esq.’”? When he found
in the package only some scraps of dirty brown
paper, Gove lost his temper and hurried back to
New York, and having secured the arrest of Ed-
ward Harkins and Henry Palmer, was himself de-
tained as a witness until Saturday, when the trio
appeared before Justices Dowling and Shandley at
the Special Sessions.

The colossal Abe H. Hummel, who appeared in
- the interest of the counterfeiters, insisted that Gove
was as great a scoundrel as the prisoners.

Gove, after telling his story to the Court, was
subjected to a rigid cross-examination. He said:

‘Tam a peddler; am not married; go to church
sometimes; did not come here to buy counterfeit
money; was on my way to Albany. The letter

was addressed to my name, but was not for me;
only went to Owens out of curiosity. I expected
to get $100 for $15.”

‘Did you expect $100 in counterfeit money 2”

Peddler—‘‘T expected $100.”

‘Answer the question yes or no. Did you bar-
gain for and expect to get this $100 in counterfeit
money ?”?

The witness here broke down.

William Hine, in the employ cf the prisoners as
errand runner, etc., for a few days previous to the
arrest, deposed that he got a package from the
prisoner, Palmer, to take to the express office, and
after going some distance turned back, as he had
forgotten where he was sent; had sent packages
previously by express; never enquired what the
business of his employers was; thought he was in
a lawyer’s office; his salary was to be ten dollars a
week, but he received only two dollars.

The Judge commented on his innocence.

The Court failed to see the colossal Abe’s point
that Gove was as great a scoundrel as the prison-
ers, and found the latter guilty.

Justice Dowling, in passing sentence, said:
** Palmer and Harkins, from the evidence, the Court
finds you guilty. There can be no doubt that the

complainant is a very dishonorable man, but we
have to use dishonorable men to convict raseals
sometimes. You have no legitimate business.
The country is flooded with such circulars as you
send out. Country people are imposed on and
victimized every day. The Governor of this State
has written me repeatedly about such cases as this,
and the whole State is offended when an offence of
this kind is committed. The complainant is cer-
tainly not a worthy man, but the Court must in-
flict its most severe punishment when the evidence
is as direct as in this case. You took money and
gave nothing inreturn. The sentence of the Court
is that you each be confined in the Penitentiary for
six months, and each pay a fine of $50, and stand
committed until paid.’

[All good citizens are in duty bound to assist in
hunting down, and in shutting up in prison, every
one of these wicked creatures. Let not one escape. —
They are enemies of the race, and must be rooted
out. Help, help catch the rogues! |

THE CONVERSION OF St. Pav. Three discourses
by Geo. Garvis Geer, D.D., Rector of St. Timothy’s
Church, New York. 8. R. Wells, 889 Broadway,
New York, 1871. pp. 82. Price, $1.00.

There is not a little clearness about these Ser-
mons, in which the writer draws out the teachings
of St, Paul’s Conversion, in reference to present
opponents of the faith. In the first he takes St.
Paul’s Conversion as a standing witness, that there
is and must be such a thing as a truth to be con-
verted to. In the second he deals with the case of
those who expect to be converted by some sudden
miracle, and thus misapply the history of St. Paul,
‘‘ waiting,’’ as Dr. Geer says, ‘‘to be flattered by a
special invitation, and interference on the part of
Heaven.’’ In the third he argues that the fact of
St. Pauls being referred by God to Ananias for
Baptism and for teaching, shows the value to be
put upon the regular means of grace in the church.
The sermons are thoroughly useful as well as
sound,

The following extract from a private

letter, received at this office, and written without
any expectation that the parties named would ever
see it, we print as a well merited testimonial of the
integrity and ability of the gentlemen comprising
the extensive clothing establishment of Messrs.
Freeman and Burr. Their advertisement on an-
other page we commend to the attention of our
readers.

‘In regard to Freeman & Burr, and my experience
with them, I would say, that seeing their card in
the Journal, I wrote them for samples, etc., and
received some fifty, together with a pamphlet fash-
ion plate, and several blanks, with minute direc-
tions for self-measurement. Finding the prices
nearly fifty per cent. less than those charged.
here, [the writer is a resident of Cheyenne, Wyom-
ing Territory,] for similar qualities of goods, I.
immediately sent them an order for a good over-
coat, and a suit of black. * * * Jn due time I.
received the goods all right, and upon trial was
delighted to find that every garment was a. perfect,
fit. Not only better than I expected, but better on
the whole than I remember having received from any
tailor where I was personally present. The garments
were well made, and as near as I could judge,.
strictly according to sample.”’

WHAT TO EAT AND DRINK.

Vegetarians, Bible-Christians and Temperance
Reformers will be interested in the life of the late
Rey. WM. METCALF® (for sale at this office), who,
for more than forty years, lived the life of a strict
vegetarian. He was fifty two years a preacher, and
died at the age of 75. Thelittle book gives an ac-
count of his birth, education, theological studies,
adoption of the vegetarian dict, his study of medi-
cine, and graduation as an M. D.; he became an
editor; correspondence with Drs. Gitanie a, Alcott,
Simpson, etc. ; formation of the American Vegetar-
ian Society ; establishes the Bible-Christian Church,
his Marriage; visit to England; return to Amer-
ica; continues his lecturing, preaching, writing,
etc., always in the interest of these themes, Veg-
etarianism, Temperance, Religion, and Godliness.
The little book before us—which sells for 25 cents—
gives the story of his earnest useful life, and happy,
though much lamented death,

How to Harn a Frew Dotzars. Self
Helpfulness, is a characteristic of every well con-
stituted human being. Every one who can prefers
to earn his or her support, rather than fecl depend-
ent on, or beholden to another. Even the little child
asks permission to help, in one way or another.
This is natural. Now there are ‘grown up’’ Boys
and Girls, who have almost nothing todo. Their
wants, already numerous, are increasing, and the
money to supply them even with the necessary
reading matter to keep their minds growing, is not
always furnished; the means to clothe their bodies
tastefully, may not be available when wanted.
Let us suppose these young folks have grown to
man’s estate. They now require a hundred little
things, not absolutely necessary, perhaps, to keep
body and soul together, but to adorn, improve, or
to beautify, for which they do not like to ask
money from parents or guardians. If they could
only earn the means, what a satisfaction it would be.
We have considered this whole matter and devised
a way by which relief and comparative indepen-
dence may be attained, at least by those who have
spirit, enterprise, preseverance, and are not too
timid. Is it lady-like? Yes. Is it honest and
honorable? Yes. Well pray tell me what itis? [We
have just printed a circular entitled ‘‘ How To EARN
A Few Douuars.”’ giving the details of this plan ;
this will be sent on receipt of stamp to pre-pay
postage. Address this office. |

Already a number of ladies have acted on this
most liberal proposition and are using the money for
some useful charity, buying a Sunday-school libra-
ry, @ sewing machine for a poor widow, an organ
for a church, a public library, or putting a few dol-
lars in their own pockets, to pay for summer excur-
sions, etc. ‘If wishes were horses, we would all
take a ride.” Wishing alone will not bring sup-
plies, but put a little earnest work with your
wishes, and it will tell. There is no risk, no capi-
tal required; only a good tongue, some confidence,
more perseverance, and a determination to sueceed.
The circular will tell nll about it.

Disrrisute Taem.—lIt is a real kind-

the best results. A professor in one of our colleges

No Imevosters, no swindlers, no medi-
cal quacks, nor ‘‘blind”’ cheats, can get into the
pages of this Journal—except to be exposed.
Advertisers, who do a legitimate business, appreci-
ate this, for they do not like to be ‘‘mixed up”
with rogues. It is the duty of publishers to pro-
tect their readers, as far as possible, against im-
posters, How many do it? We find Religious
Newspapers opening their broad sheets to: the
most filthy’quackery! Is this really using the
Devil to serve the Lord?

Whatever is true, useful, and proper to be adver-
tised, we have no objection to placing before our
readers. Whatever is untrue and deceitful we feel
in duty bound to expose. Advertisers may feel as-
sured of two things, namely, we shall try to keep
out all bad advertisers, and to place the good ones
before a large and liberal class of intelligent
readers.

“CATCH THEM.”

Editor of ‘‘ The Phrenological Journal,’’—Dear
Sir -—I read and have read your Journal for a long
time. There is no subject that I am fonder of than
Phrenology. ‘‘The proper study of mankind is
man; but mankind could not pursue the investi-
gation successfully till those great benefactors of
the human race—Gall, Spurzheim and Combe—arose
to dispel the twilight, through which even Physio-
logists viewed the subject. I had just got through
the study of medicine, preparatory to practice,
when Combe’s work fell into my hands, about 1882.

In the destruction of my house and all its con-
tents, I lost a large medical and miscellaneous
library, including literary, philosophical and prac-
tical works, what I can never replace, and which I
would not have time to read, though I am now in
my 66th year. In your May number there is an
article on counterfeit money dealers. Their letters
and propositions have been extensively urged upon
the attention of men of every occupation here—in
the South—including clergymen.

In a few cases they have induced the persons
addressed to accept their propositions. An acquain-
tance of mine doing business in this place—Winns-
boro—was simple enough to write them on the
subject, and they sent a box by express, which he
was also foolish enough to pay 120 dollars to the
express agent here for. It contained nothing but
shavings and some old iron. The name (probably
assumed) of the person and address, who sent it is
Wm. Wade & Co., No. 59 Cedar Street, New York.
I should presume the express agent in N. Y., by
reference to his books, could ascertain the person
who delivered the package addressed to OL
Winnsboro, 8. C. Any information as to the
possibility or probability of tracing the rascal up
and punishing him for his crimes would be properly
appreciated. Please let us have the benefit of your
exertions and oblige, yours respectfully, —-——.

The money, $120 was sent from this place March
29th. You need not expose the name of the per-
son in your Journal, who got the package.

WINNSBORO, 8. C.

While we sympathize with our South Carolina
correspondent, (or his friend the dupe,) we cannot
encourage him in the hope of either getting his
money back, or of catching the rogue. The express
companies receive and forward bundles, boxes and
packages delivered to them by unknown men,
women or children, knowing nothing of their con-
tents, whether gold, silver, iron, sand or shayings.
Their business is to forward and C. O. D. (i. e.,
collect on delivery). Ifa rogue orders counterfeit
money, he will probably get sand, shavings, scrap-
iron, or other rubbish, and it serves him right.
Only rogues would invest in such an undertaking.
Is not ‘‘ honesty the best policy ?”

Exrract oF Mrat.—Prof. Liebig dis-
covered a method of extracting the nutritious
qualities of meat, by which forty-five pounds of
beef are made into one pound of extract. Cattle
on the immense plains of Texas can be raised very
cheaply. Taking advantage of this fact, a concern,
of which Mr. Glanz, 194 William St., N.Y., is Sole
Agent, have established themselves in that country,

and are manufacturing Extract of Meat by Liebig’s
process. It is said to be valuable in all depart-
ments of cookery where beef can be made ayail-
able, and is much cheaper. Further information
can be obtained by addressing the agent as above.

SarEms.— The improvements in the
manufacture of both fire and burglar proof safes in
the past twenty years have been very great. At the
present time no safe makers stand higher than
Messrs. Marvin & Co., of this city. Mr. Marvin
has devoted the best part of his life to the work of
constructing a safe which should be literally Firz
PROOF. The firm claim to have taken out more
patents for improvements in safes than any other
concern in the country. Their safes are filled with
alum and dry plaster of Paris, which is claimed to
be superior to any other. Alum contains by chem-
ical analysis, 55 per cent. of pure water. In case
of fire this water is converted into steam which,
with the plaster of Paris preserves the safe. Besides,
these safes are always perfectly dry inside. The
firm also manufactures improved burglar proof
safes. Parties interested can receive a beautifully
illustrated catalogue, giving full particulars, by
addressing the manufacturers with stamp. See
advertisement. .

Here is the view of a most useful, durable, and
good-looking chimney cap, invented by Mr. E.
Myrick, of Groton Junction, Mass. It is made of
east iron, is cheap, easily put up, and will last a
life-time.

It is well known that the top bricks, (and fre-
quently in a very short time, ) become loose and work
off, and many times drop down the flue, and lodge
in such a way as to stop the draft, and can only be
removed at much trouble and expense. And when
they fall outside on slated roofs they break the
slate, and do other damage many times far exceed-
ing the cost of capping the chimney.

Added to the unsightly appearance of a dilapidat-
ed Chimney, the displaced brick causes the draft to
be irregular, often blowing down the chimney, and
sending the smoke into the room. Such chimneys
are generally left a long time before being repaired,
it being a disagreeable, difficult and expensive job
to do.

This new iron cap corrects all these difficulties,
and presents an ornamental object to the eye.
Send a stamp, as above, for circular with full par-
ticulars.

AN IMPORTANT WORK—WNew Bai ition.

Tur PARENTS’ GuIpDE; or Human Development
through Inherited Tendencies. By Mrs. Hester
Pendleton. Second edition, revised and enlarged.
One vol. 12mo. Price $1.50. 8. R. WELus, Pub-
lisher, 889 Broadway, New York.

As the author fitly says in the preface, ‘this
book disarms criticism,” for its subject is one of
such vast importance, the method adopted in pre-
| senting it is so clear and unassuming, and the tes-
timony adduced so convincing—the facts at once
striking home to the consciousness of every intelli-
gent reader—that no true man, Z. e., one who has
the welfare of his race at heart, could peruse its
pages without becoming sympathetically impress-
ed by the earnest purpose and benevolent zeal of
the author. Mrs. Pendleton gives the results of
many years observation, and the deductions from
extensive reading in her book, with reference to the
transmission of mental and physical characteristics
from parents to children. She treats this peculiarly
difficult subject with great delicacy, and yet with
that firmness which so vitally important a topic
demands; she seeks to meet the situation fairly
and squarely, as she finds it in domestic life at large
and bestow what she can of admonition, sugges-
tion, or encouragement. Society is weighed down
and oppressed by the great numbers of the deform-
ed, the deaf, the dumb, the blind, the insane, the
idiotic, those depraved in organization, and those
whose extreme susceptibilities render them objects
of constant anxiety to friends. In the ‘‘ Parents’
Guide” we find such unfortunates carefully con-
sidered, and the probable or critical causes of their
defective organization indicated. The book is
burdened by no technical phrases, but written ina
terse clear style for the masses, and to the masses
it is most cordially commended. The following
is-a synopsis of its contents :
1.—Object of the writer in preparing this Book;
Transmission of Characteristics, from Parent to

Child, Governed by Law; Possibilities of Parental
Influence; Natural Improvement; Genius Inborn.

Mother of Napoleon; Patrick Henry and his Moth-
er; Parentage ot Franklin.

3.—Maternal Traits Inherited ; Examples; Lord
Byron; Cuvier; ‘‘ The Strong are Born of the
Strone, and the Good of the Worthy ’’; The Moth-
er of Washington.

4,—Marriage of Near Relatives ; Peculiarities in
the Transmission of Characteristics.

able Effect; Effects of Intemperance ; Need of

ation in producing Malformations.

its Different Forms; Excessive Mental Activity,

a JOURNAL MISCHLLANY.

TuHoucutTs FoR THE YounG Men, and
for the Young Women of America; or, a few
practical words of advice. By L. U. Reavis.
With the Ideal Man and the Ideal Woman, by
Horace GREELEY. One vol., #2mo. Price §1.
New York: 8S. R. WELLS, 889 Broadway.

The object of this work is to encourage those
whose opportunities have not been favorable, and
to guide them by honorable purpose and earnest
endeavor, to rise above the embarrassments of
their condition, and thus call out all that is noble
and Godlike in their nature, thereby securing de-
velopment and culture as a desirable object in it-
self, and at the same time winning respect, fortune
and renown. It takes hold of the home duties
and virtues with ungloved hands and an untram-
melled tongue, and talks to the Sons and Daugh-
ters of America as an earnest, honest, well-in-
formed father would do, There is an important
chapter on Self-Education; another on the Forma-
tion of Character; one on Marriage; What Ben.
Franklin Said of It; on Politics; Our Duties to
the Government; on Religion; concluding with
the ‘‘ ideal Man of the Future,’’ by Horace Gree-
ley, in which he treats of Cleanliness, Physical De-
velopment, Temperance, Knowledge of Natural
Law, Labor a Source of Enjoyment, Independence,

etc., and Horace Mann’s celebrated Letter to a |

Young Lawyer.

The second part, or Thoughts for the Young
Women of Amcrica, contains, Ist, the Ways of
Life; Industry; Education; What to Read; the
Formation of Character; Labor, or What Shall I

Do?; Marriage; on Religion; General Advice as to |

Self-culture, etc.; concluding with ‘The Ideal
Woman,’’ by Horace Greeley; Orsini to his
Daughters; and a poem, ‘* Will You Love Me
When Lam Old?” It isa real satisfaction to ad-
dress words of kind encouragement to young peo-
ple, who have their way to work up in the world.
For the want of this, many become discouraged,
and content themselves with life on a lower plain
than nature intended them to live. Our author
“has been there,’? and speaks from experience.
He dedicates the combined book respectively to
Mr. John 8. Loomis and to Miss Anna E. Dickin-

son, each of whom represent the class of young |

men and women addressed. We commend the
warm, affectionate, judicious and sympathetic
words of the author to the attention of all readers,
with the assurance that it will do them good.

in contact therewith as readily through the volume
of water which is constantly passing off, as through
the medium of the iron tubing, which affords the
only means of transmitting this property, or effect,
in most of the so-called Magnetic wells. This
well has gained its wonderful reputation by test
and experiment, without any of the usual aids of
interested laudation or paid professional commen-
dation, and the first systematic effort to bring it
into general notice by publishing some of the facts
concerning its peculiarities and performances is
now being made by Wm. Jenny, Esq., the Agent,
who will on application, send free of charge to all
applicants, a pamphlet containing the full particu-

¢

lars concerning the cures it has effected.”

We will not “‘ throw cold water’’ on this new as-
pirant for fame and fortune, nor hinder broken down
invalids from resorting to the magnetic waters for
relief, but simply suggest that all pure water and
all pure air is magnetic. Rheumatism, paralysis,
dyspepsia, and other infirmities may be eradicated,
by plenty of good air, water, exercise, rest, sleep,
food and other hygienic agencies. But there are
no ‘‘ curative’ properties in pure, mineral, or other
waters. -

S. R. Weis, Esq.—-Dear Sir, May 11th, 1871.
For the past twenty years I have resorted to advertis-
ing in the public journals more or less, as a medium cal-
culated to extend my business. About three years ago I
ordered a short advertisement inserted in the PHRENO-
LOGICAL JOURNAL, and as I did not have much faith in
the advertisement at the time, I was greatly surprised at
receiving business letters from every ae of the country,
even from the British Provinces, the majority of the
writers mentioning the fact that they saw my notice
in the above mentioned JouRNAL. About this time
I visited Europe with my friend, Ole Bull, and was absent
several months. Upon arriving home my wife called my
attention to the fact of there being a ‘‘ bushel of letters”
for me, and said she ‘‘hey have been coming all Sunvmer.”
I thought this ratber strange, as I had only ordered the
advertisement in for one month, and I can account for
this result only in the following marner. The ‘* PHRENO-
LOGICAL JOURNAL”? ig not torn up immediatcly afer one
reading, as is the case with newspapers generally; it is
laid on the Center Table, or, perhaps, loaned to a friend.
And as it is in d00k-furm, it is of course preserved and
read and re-read, and becomes a sort of standard litera-
ture. I am free to say that after having advertised in
the most prominent journals of the day, the ‘‘ PHRENO-
LOGICAL JOURNAL’? and ‘‘ POMEROY’s WEEKLY DEMO-
craT,’’ have given me the best results, the profit on one
order received through the Phrenological Journal more
than paid the cost ofadvertisement. J. JAY WATSON.

4 JOURNAL MISCHLLANY.

Tue Parents’ Guipz; or, Human Devel-
opment through Inherited Tendencies. By Mrs.
Hester PENDLETON. Second edition, revised
and enlarged. 12mo, price $1.50. Published by
8. R. Wells, 389 Broadway, New York.

< More than twenty-five years ago, the author of
this excellent work, issued a volume entitled
“Mental and Moral Qualities Transmissible from
Parents to Offspring.’? The wide circulation of
that work among a class of readers the most moral
and intelligent which the country can boast, has
made the name of Hester Pendleton very widely
and favorably known. That name has not been
trumpeted in the newspapers. The subject was
one of deep interest and earnestness, containing
valuable facts for those who felt the need of them ;
but the great mass of the world has not known or
eared that such a book existed. Moreover, the
work was one to be spoken of quietly by friend to
friend, rather than to be spoken of by some flashy
sensational paper. Time has ripened the author ;
time has developed much truth in the line of her
early investigation and publication. The world is
now more full of material for the perfecting of her
work, which she has wisely and well done, in the
handsome volume before us.

The proper way to review this work is to give
it, page by page. It should be read to be fully ap-
preciated. A glance at the table of contents
would give any inquisitive student a hunger to
peruse it thoroughly. One chapter leads off with
“Mental Traits Inherited; the Strong are Born
of the Strong, and the Good of the Worthy; Mar-
riage of Near Relatives; Causes of Disease and
Imbecility.”’> Another contains, ‘“‘ Transmission
of Disease.” Another speaks of ‘‘ Physical De-
bility upon Offspring.’”’ Various social evils are
enumerated in another chapter. ‘‘ Causes of In-
sanity among the ignorant, and also among the
educated ; Why the Sons of Great Men are Sel-
dom Great,’ etc. The work is full of cases in
point. Some of the most marked historical char-
acters are introduced ; their ancestry, the cireum-
stances of their birth and training are set forth.
Every page of the book has something in it which
every father and every mother, or those proposing
to become such, would be profited to read.

The drift and spirit of the book is delicate and |

modest, but plain and earnest. The style of the
composition is smooth, compact, and correct.
The aim of the author is high, as the perusal of
her book will readily show. We trust it will be
largely circulated, and attentively read, and we
doubt not much good to the race will be the result.

Guanaco UmBreiias.— Many have,
no doubt, seen the mystic word, ‘‘GUANACO”’ and
wondered at its meaning. Guanaco is an animal
of the Camel family, which inhabits the Andes
Mountains, in South America. It is celebrated for
its wool or hair, which is very fine, lustrous and
long, often measuring twelve to eighteen inches in
length. The natives use this hair for making stock-
ings, gloves, cloaks, etc., and some of the garments
made from it are of so fine a texture as to sell for
$500, and upwards. The fleece of the Guanaco is
free from ticks and other parasitic insects, and is so
impervious to water, that it is almost impossible
to wet them to the skin.

Messrs. IsAAc SmiTH’s Son & Co., 405 Broad-
way, New York, have introduced the cloth made
from the hair of this animal as an UMBRELLA
covering. It has a fine silky appearance, will not
fade, and is said to be water-proof. This firm are
the sole manufacturers of Umbreilas, made from
this material, and purchasers should be careful to
see that their name and trade-mark ‘‘ Guanaco”’
appear on the inside of each one. These umbrellas are
more QGurable than silk, and cost one third less.
See advertisement in another column.

A Goop Pusiic ENTERTAINMENT.
Amid the numerous public exhibitions, and enter-
tainments which feed the prurient tastes of the
public, and reflect an unhealthy influence upon ail
who attend them, it is refreshing to find one which
does not pander to the prevailing thirst for low sen-
sation. We allude to that chaste, and really beauti-
fu. entertainment given by the Berger Family,
whose singular musical skill surprises and delights
every audience, Their excellence is particularly
shown in their specialty as Bell Ringers. Certainly
we never before heard such melody and harmony
produced with bells. A very important and to us in-
teresting feature of these entertainments is the
physiognomical delineations of Mr. Russell. This
gentleman has a protean countenance which is
capable of exhibiting every phase of expression,
and seemingly loses its own identity completely at
times. We may print an article ere long with en-
graved illustrations, showing Mr. Russell’s power
over his face.

ProtuREs—How To Comt.—Never

come in a hurry or a flurry. ed takes black, and
red faces take black. Moreover, if you are pushed
for time, your Pictures will present a worn and
wearied expression, which you will not like, and
which will compel you to take the time for another
sitting. Arrange matters at the office, or the shop,
or at home, or with your creditors, so that you ean
take it P-H-R-F-H-C-T-L-Y H-A-S-Y qauring the
operations of waiting your turn and the making
of your picture. If you do, the likeness will be
calm, peaceful, and true to you, and you will feel
repaid for your tranquillity. Ladies who have
shopping and an engagement with the photograph-
er on the same day, will please be careful to attend
to the latter first.—Bogardus.

Save SexEps.—Our lady readers
should not forget to save seeds from their best
flowering plants and carefully label and put them
away for planting. If those who love flowers
would saye seed in Autumn, they would have less
occasion to purchase in spring—Aforticulturist.

The same may be said of many other seeds such
as cherry, plum, etc. Millions of acres in the West
await fruit seeds, which friends in the east should
send to friends in the West. Save the seeds.

“SAFETY Orn.”—Serious accidents re-
sulting from the use of impure Kerosene oil are of
almost daily occurrence. One can seareely take up
a paper without reading of one or more explosions

| of Kerosene lamps, attended often with loss of

life and property. The remedy for this distressing
state of things, is simple and lies in the hands of
every family making use of this oil for iftuminating
purposes. It is never safe to use an oil that is not
How are we to know
the pure from the impure article you say? First,
never buy a cheap oil. Oils that are retailed for

| thirty to forty cents a gallon cannot he pure. Ben-

zine is the explosive property of Kerosene oil and
where this substance enters largely into the com-
position of oils, as is the ease with all that are sold
at a low price, they cannot be safe. The second

| precaution is to see that the name of the Refiner

appears prominently on the barrel or can eontain-
if he is not known to you reijeet the
oil. Unscrupulous dealers often assert that the
cheaper oils are just as good but such is not the
ease. There are several parties in this city who are
making most excellent oil. Among the most promi-
nent of these are DensLow & BusH whose adver-
tisement of the ‘‘Safety’’ oil appears in another
column. The people can rely on this as a perfectly
safe oil. The cost is a trifle more as it retails for
sixty cents a gallon but surely no one would hvsi-
tate to pay a few cents monthly for an oil which is
guaranteed not to explode. That the public may
not have an inferior article imposed on them, this
oil is put up in cans with the name ‘‘ Denslow and
Bush’s Safety Oil,” stamped thereon.

FOR NEXT YEAR! GET READY!

Already, publishers are putting forth their an-
nouncements, promising ‘‘great things’’ for 1872.
Flaming posters, exciting hand bills, and circulars,
with testimonials, certifying to the excellence of
this immense story paper; that tremendous mag-
azine; and the other splendid family illuminator!
No chamber-maid, milliner, cook, washerwoman,
“or any other man,” can possibly exist without
it. We hold our breath, in view of the tremendous
offers made by generous publishers, who are so
anxious to give away something for nothing. “A
splendid musical wind instrument, with several
smali holes in it, which you can blow in,—worth
six cents,—given for four new subscribers! Take
it quick, or all will be gone.”’ Miss Smart writes all
the time exclusively for this brilliant Borealis,—or,
pore-us-all,—and all who take the paper will never
need to take anything else, and soforth. Modesty
becomes some folks, but publishers prefer—Green-
backs, with pay in advance.

THE PHRENOLOGICAL JOURNAL has to do with
brains, not brass, and men of common sense read
it. Imagination and the affections have their
uses, but the ‘‘ warp and woof”’ of human life,
human duty and human happiness is not made up
of neither love-sick twaddle, nor of blood and
thunder stories. With us, who make human life
and character a constant study, time here on earth
seems all too short, to be frittered away in the read-
ing of such stuff, as is turned out by the ton, and
sold te thoughtless youth. O, the damage which
is done by literary voluptuaries—not to use a harsh-
er term,—is almost inconceivable. By them thous-
ands are perverted, and wreck and ruin are the re-
sults.

It is no merit in this JourNnaL to avoid such a
course. We deem it nothing less than criminal, in
any one, to place in the hands of innocent youth,
such reading matter as will excite and pervert a
pure mind. But we can only sound the alarm, give
the word of warning and leave it for parents,
guardians and teachers, to select the sort of reading
matter most useful for both children and adults.

This JouRNAL has a mission of its own; its
character is well established; it will be true to its
principles, and if it fail in any respect, it will be

from an error of judgment, and not from a bad
motive. If our friends, who intend to re-subscribe,
will make it a point to induce their friends and
neighbors to join them, it will prove most accept-
able to us. Readers wish to have the JoURNAL’S
sphere of usefulness enlarged. They can secure
this by speaking a timely word in its behalf. Clubs
for 1872 may be started at once, so that none can
say when solicited to subscribe, *‘ too late.”?> The
most profitable reading is not that which inflames
the passions, excites and preverts the senses, or
misleads minds seeking knowledge. It is that
which puts one in the way of knowing himself,
his faults, capabilities, ete. That which enables
one to read his fellow men at a glance, and that, too,
on scientific principles. In short, that which EN-
COURAGES every one to make the most of himself,
and to help improve and lift up his fellow men.
To all such the PHRENOLOGICAL JOURNAL may be
earnestly commended.

Now Reavy, our Annual of Phrenol-
ogy and Physiognomy for 1872—illustrated. We
copy the introduction as follows:

In presenting our Eran1H ANNUAL to the public,
it is a pleasing reflection that the cause to which
it is devoted is steadily progressing. There is a
very general acceptance of Phrenology, especially
when it is based on and combined with anatomy,
physiology, and physiognomy, and when separated
from the absurd claims and teachings of ignorant
charlatans and self-styled professors. In fact, the
chief drawback to the advancement of Phrenology
has consisted in its pretended advocacy by those
miserable ‘‘ wolves in sheep’s clothing,’ commonly
known as astrologers, fortune-tellers, etc., who
have left their ugly tracks wherever they have been.
Thoroughly bad themselves, they have atempted to
to drag down Phrenology to their own low level.

Another impediment to its diffusion is found in
the ignorance, prejudice, and bigotry of those
small-minded persons who can take in no new
ideas. Having attained their mental growth, they
are at a ‘‘stand-still,”’ or in a state of dotage.
They will admit for truth nothing which was not
taught to them in their childhood; while all live,
intellizent, fair-minded men and women every-
where exhibit a liberal, candid attitude toward
new revelations, whether in science or intellectual
philosophy.

Just now the principles of Phrenology are being
applied not only to the discernment of character,
but to the choice of pursuits, to the classification
of children in schools according to temperament
and natural capacity, and to the management of
idiots, imbeciles, and to the treatment of the insane
and criminal,

Clergymen also find it useful in analyzing and
interpreting those questions which were hitherto
only mysterics. Editors make use of our nomen-
elature, which is admitted on all hands to be most
appropriate and effective. How full of meaning,
for example, is that word Self-Esteem, or that
other, Combativeness! and so on through the list,
including Comparison, Benevolence, Veneration,
Firmness, Language, Time, Tune, and the rest.
We grant that some modifications seem necessary
to a more perfect system, and instead of the term
Destructiveness, which represents a perverted con-
dition, we would adopt aterm which should express
its normal condition, viz., Exeeutiveness; while
Marvelousness should be called Spirituality, or the
organ of Faith. But, in the main, the names of
the organs are in keeping with their function.
Each mental function has its faculty, as each
function of the body has its organ, as the heart for
circulating the blood, the lungs for respiration, the
stomach for digesting food, the eye for seeing, the
ear f( heariac, the tongue for tasting, and so
pn.

These puints have all been discussed elsewhere,

and the correctness of location, as well as of name
and function, is established beyond controversy.
Our present duty is to disseminate a knowledge of
these truths, to bring them to the attention of the
race. If the Gospel is to be preached to all the
world, so also are the truths of science to go hand
in hand with revelation, the one in harmony with
the other. There is no incompatibility between
one truth and another, for ‘‘truth squares with
truth on every side.”’ We think with the immor-
tal Spurzheim, ‘‘ True religion is central truth, and
all knowledge should be gathered around it.”

Our knowledge is not yet complete, nor is. it
likely to become so while we remain finite beings.
But it is our privilege and our duty to learn, to in-
vestigate, and to acquire all the knowledge we can,
and to apply it for the edification, improvement,
and elevation of mankind.

Go forth, little ANNUAL! impress those who are,
impressible, encourage the faltering, confirm and
strengthen those in the line of duty, correct the
habits of the perverted and dissipated, and assist
the reader in discovering and obeying the laws of
his being. [See table of contents, on another page. }

Tus Srertmne [ron Ore.—This iron
ore bed, recently opened, is announced as one o
the most valnable in the world. The ore has been
fully tested, and proved to be a Lenticular Red
Hematite. It weighs about three tons to the cubie
yard; overlaid by four or five feet of earth; be-
neath this is about a foot thickness of good lime-
stone, easily removed; and beneath this still, are
two inches of slate or shale, when the clear iron
ore is presented.

It is located in Sterling, Cayuga Co., N. Y., near
the Junction of the Southern Central; Oswego
and Lake Ontario Shore Railroads, about one
mile from the shore of Ontario Bay, at Fair Haven.

The ore is now being earried to this port and
from there shipped to the west and the east
through Lake Ontario and the Canals. The South-
ern Central R.R. is to be pushed on to completion
at once, which will connect this point with the
coal fields of Penn.; when this is done, large
furnaces will be erected and the ore turned into
iron on the spot. These iron deposits are likely to
prove very rich and extensive. Indieations of Salt
and Sulphur springs are also found in the town.
