Corizs to “Give Away.” — Good
friends of this JouRNAL, who wish to have it read
in every family, sometimes order—and pay for—
ten, twenty and even fifty numbers, to give away.
They regard this the best way to introduce it.
Those who read one number will want to read
more. It has been said that anything which is
cosiless, is worthless, to the possessor, but we do
not admit this to be true. One may possess a rough
diamond, which, on being lapidaried, becomes of
great’ value. So, one not acquainted with the
claims or principles of Phrenology may look on
the contents of this JouRNAL as something above
or beyond his comprehension. But, if he will open
the door which leads to a knowledge of the human
mind, through its many faculties and organs of
Brain and Body, he will become so fascinated with
its study that he will wish to read more deeply,
and learn from the JouRNAL all he can. We will
furnish at cost any number of copies to “ give
away,” that the reader may wish. Each number
is stereotyped, and we will reprint, if necessary, to
supply any demand.

“Goop Books For Atu.”—Now that
the summer is past and the harvest is ended, it is a
good time for readers to re-stock their Libraries.
Looking over the numerous catalogues one will be
puzzled to select just what he wants or needs. It
will be safe to begin by striking out what he does
not want. It is simply foolish to lumber up one’s
shelves with literary trash,—such as floods the
country—when he may secure ‘‘ the Best Thoughts
of the Best Minds’ at the same price. When about
it select ‘‘ Book which are Books,”’ and leave the
foolish fiction for fools. When a really useful Book
is brought to the notice of a sensible person he will
desire to possess it, and instead of the question
“can I afford it,’ it will be ‘‘can I afford to do
without it??? We are assured by our agents, that
they almost invariably receive hearty thanks from
those to whom they sell owr publications. Why ?
because they are indeed, ‘‘good Books for all.’

PHRENOLOGY RECOGNIZED BY PUBLIC
Merw.—We take no part in the personal controver-
sy between Messrs. Butler of Massachusetts, and
The one may be all his
enemies say of him, and the other all his friends
say of him. We are interested in the fact that the
principles of Phrenology are applied by one to the
other. Here is what Mr. Hawley says of Mr. But-

PHoNnoGRAPHY, or Short-hand Writing.

We frequently have occasion to answer questions
bearing on the subject of Phonography, which are
to the following purport:
_ (1.) How long does it take to learn Phonogra-
phy? (2.) What are the best manuals, or text-
books ? (3.) What do they cost ? and can you fur-
nish them? (4.) Is a teacher necessary, and can
you aid me in procuring one? (5.) Can I easily
find a situation when I have mastered the art?
(6.) Who employ short-hand writers ?

In general terms we reply to the first question.
The facility with which this most valuable art is
acquired, depends upon one’s mental capacity.
Some take hold of it perseveringly, and in four
months are competent to perform the part of
an amanuensis, being able to write sixty or even
more words per minute, and subsequent practice .
gives them more skill. Others may not be able
to acquire such proficiency in six, eight or ten
months. It is quite certain however that three
months of honest study will prove one’s aptitude
for short-hand. To become a verbatim report-
er requires considerable practice, but whoever
makes good progress in learning the simpler or cor-
responding form of short-hand need not despair of
reaching that lofty position in the art. 2d. A list of
the best books is given on another page. All have
been in use for years, and found sufficient. Pit-
man’s works are the longest in the field, Munson’s
the shortest time. American short-hand writers
vary in their preferences, but Phonographers of
eminence are found in the Pitman, Graham and
Munson schools. 3d. As regards the cost, a glance
through the list will disclose that, and also the fact
of our being able to supply them, 4th. This art may
be acquired without a teacher, but his instruction
is a great aid, particularly in the rudiments of
short-hand. We have facilities for giving lessons
by mail, a plan at once convenient for those ata
distance from the city, and found to be eminently
successful. Terms for a full course of twelve les-
sons, $10. 5th. There is no acquirement which wi
more readily procure an opening for a young man
seeking employment than the ability to write short-
hand, and certainly none so remunerative at the
very beginning. One of fair education and good
habits, and capable of filling the part of an aman-
uensis may draw from 8 to 25 dollars a week, ac-
cording to the length of time he has been employ-
ed, and the nature of the work. 6th. Short-hand
writers are now employed not only in the profes-
sions, but in almost every department of business.
They are indispensable to the newspapers and in
judicial proceedings, while merchants, bankers,
railroad men, and all others who have much writ-
ing to do, find it greatly to their advantage to em-
ploy the ready pep of the short-hand writer. By
his aid they are enabled to dispatch threc times as
much work as by the old method, and in a far more
satisfactory manner.

Our ADVERTISEMENTS.—It is interest-
ing, not only to look over the advertising pages,
but to read them. How crisp and compact they
are, every word tells. If those who write for the
press, would take the pains our advertisers do to put
‘“much in little,” there would be no dull reading,
no going to sleep while reading. Observe how em-
phatic and magnetic the expressions of a wide-
awake business man are in his advertisements. One
can easily tell whether or not the advertiser is tell-
ing the truth; whether he magnifies, or is modest
or arrogant. Read the advertisements, study char-
acter, and learn a useful lesson.

Lost or Sro.en.—It is always pain-
ful to suspect another of theft, or even of careless-
ness. But the frequent losses by post, leave no
other alternative. We strongly suspect—though
we cannot always prove dishonesty, on the part of
some of those who convey our letters—now and
then, some one connected with the post-office de-
partment is detected stealing letters—with their
contents—and is sentenced to states prison. It
comes out that the thief kept fast company, gam-
bled or speculated and lost. But how are we to
know whom to trust ? We answer, by Phrenology,
and by all the other evidences attainable. Trust
no man who cannot show a. good, record and
whose habits are unexceptionable. It is possi-
ble, nay easy to fill our public places of trust with
honest men. Then why not do it? Why place
thieves and robbers in charge of our property ? An
honest postmaster has not only no objection to a

rigid investigation into his character, and fitness

for the place, but he is desirous that all others shall
also be honest, and suited to the place. Weed out

the rogues, and the letters will go through to their.

destinations.
